---
title: "What's Xorq?"
description: "Xorq's three parts: an IR for pipelines, a ledger of reviewed entries, and a command-line tool that runs them"
icon: "info-circle"
headline: "Learn what Xorq is and why it exists"
---

Xorq is three interlinked things, plus the interfaces built on them:

1. **An IR.** An agent-native intermediate representation for cross-engine,
   composable, cacheable, declarative execution. A pipeline is an expression
   that compiles to many engines, caches at any node, and composes with other
   expressions.
2. **A ledger.** The IR makes every pipeline a durable artifact that's cheap to
   verify: one computation, defined before it runs, named by a hash of its
   definition, with lineage a person can read alongside it. The ledger steers
   agent work. An agent selects a reviewed entry instead of re-deriving it from
   source files.
3. **A command-line tool.** It governs execution against the ledger: build,
   add, run, check-sources, pin, rebase, compose. Arbitrary compute enters the
   deterministic system through UDXFs, Python functions that exchange Arrow
   tables over Flight.

The interfaces on top serve different users. The command-line tool doubles as
the headless mode for agents, and `xorq catalog tui` is the view for people.

## Why a ledger steers agents

[DABStep](https://huggingface.co/spaces/adyen/DABstep) is 450 data-analysis
questions over payment transaction data. With a Xorq ledger of 33 named
expressions, Haiku goes from 50% to 84%, ahead of the 75% Sonnet baseline
([Orientation Over Reasoning](https://xorq.dev/blog/orientation-over-reasoning/)).

![](/images/dabstep-benchmark.png){fig-alt="DABStep accuracy by model, Haiku at 50%, Sonnet at 75%, and Haiku with a semantic catalog at 84%"}

[Faithful, Reproducible, Wrong](https://xorq.dev/blog/faithful-reproducible-wrong/)
asks one metric question 100 times per configuration. Two of its nine
configurations run Haiku with Xorq on the same prompt. The only difference is
whether a reviewed definition of the metric was preloaded:

| | Re-derived from source files | Selected from a reviewed entry |
|---|---|---|
| Correct | 0 of 100 | 100 of 100 |
| Median turns | 21 | 4 |
| Cost per run | $0.09 | $0.02 |

## The IR

A Xorq expression is deferred: it describes the computation and runs only when
you execute it. `xo._` is the row reference, so `xo._.species` is the `species`
column of the current table.

```python
import xorq.api as xo

penguins = xo.examples.penguins.fetch()
expr = (
    penguins
    .filter(xo._.species.notnull())
    .group_by("species")
    .agg(avg_bill_length=xo._.bill_length_mm.mean())
)
```

`.cache(xo.ParquetCache.from_kwargs())` materializes any node, and
`.into_backend(xo.duckdb.connect())` moves its data to another engine. The same
expression runs on DataFusion, DuckDB, SQLite, pandas, Snowflake, Databricks,
BigQuery, Trino, Postgres, PyIceberg, and GizmoSQL. Operators exchange Arrow
RecordBatches. `xo.Pipeline.from_instance` wraps a scikit-learn pipeline whose
fit and predict steps are deferred expressions.

The expression API is inspired by Ibis. If you know pandas or SQL, it looks
familiar.

## The ledger

The ledger is a git repo on the filesystem. The command-line tool calls it a
catalog, which is why its commands live under `xorq catalog`. Aliases are
symlinks, entries are zipped builds, and metadata sidecars are plain YAML, so an
agent that clones the repo can discover everything with file operations.

An entry is a manifest plus the environment to run it. The manifest is the
content-addressed specification of the pipeline: one node per operation, each
referenced by hash, with schema, lineage, and inputs read straight off it. The
wheel and `requirements.txt` next to it let the entry run in another sandbox, on
your machine, or in production. `xorq catalog add` takes both from your project,
so it needs a `pyproject.toml` and a `uv.lock` or `requirements.txt`. Identical
computations get identical hashes, so an entry also works as a contract between
teams: they find an existing computation by name and build on it.

## The command line

Commands that act on an entry take its hash or an alias such as `prod`. When
pin, rebase, or compose produce a different pipeline, they write it as a new
entry. Entries are never edited in place, though aliases can move. By default,
writes push the ledger to its remote.

```bash
xorq catalog run prod -o out.parquet          # execute in the entry's own environment
xorq catalog check-sources prod               # did a source schema drift? reports, never repairs
xorq catalog rebase prod                      # rebuild over drifted source schemas as a new entry
xorq catalog pin prod -e --alias prod-pinned  # materialize and freeze the caches as a new entry
xorq catalog compose src transform -a pipeline  # source entry + unbound transform entry, as one
```

A UDXF is how arbitrary compute joins the system. It's a Python function from a
pandas DataFrame to a DataFrame, served behind an Arrow Flight server, that gets
named and cataloged like any other node. See the
[UDF system](udf_system.qmd).

## Who Xorq is for

Xorq is for data scientists, data engineers, ML engineers, and the agents that
work alongside them. It fits teams that:

- Write SQL-heavy pipelines but need Python for ML.
- Run the same pipeline on several engines, such as DuckDB locally and Snowflake
  in production.
- Need reproducibility and lineage for compliance or debugging.
- Want to reuse reviewed computations instead of rewriting them.

## Built on open standards

- **Apache Arrow Flight** streams Arrow data between processes.
- **Apache DataFusion** is the embedded engine for Arrow-native execution.
- **uv** builds the Python environment each entry records.

Xorq is pre-1.0. Expect breaking changes; the changelog marks them.
